adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:151 — Oversized DER ECDSA integers are truncated instead of rejected, so malformed signatures can be normalized into a valid raw signature.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that oversized DER ECDSA integers are truncated instead of rejected. Looking at the code in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java lines 147-157 (the integerToBytes method), this is actually the correct behavior for ECDSA signature conversion. When converting from ASN.1 DER format to concatenated R||S format, the BigInteger representation may have leading zeros or be larger than expected due to sign extension in two's complement representation. The truncation (taking the last qLength bytes when bytes.length > qLength) is the standard way to handle this - it removes leading zeros from the big-endian representation. This is not a security vulnerability but rather the expected normalization behavior for ECDSA signature format conversion. The code correctly handles both cases: when the integer is too large (truncate leading bytes) and when it's too small (pad with leading zeros).

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:57 — The sequence parser accepts contents that overrun the declared ASN.1 sequence length instead of rejecting malformed DER.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the readSequence() method in ASN1Decoder.java lines 49-60, the code reads the declared length, then loops while length > 0, subtracting each element's byte length. However, if the actual content bytes exceed the declared length, the loop would continue reading beyond the declared sequence boundary (since it only checks length > 0, not length >= bytes.length before subtraction). After subtraction, length could go negative, but the while condition 'length > 0' would then exit. The issue is that if bytes.length > remaining length, the code doesn't reject this as malformed - it just reads the oversized element and then exits with a negative length value. This is a valid DER parsing bug where malformed input with content exceeding declared length is not properly rejected.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Equal-priority providers are now silently selected by ServiceLoader encounter order, making the previously rejected multi-provider classpath nondeterministic.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the code changed from throwing an exception when multiple providers exist to silently selecting the first one after sorting by order(). Looking at the sorting: `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())` - providers with equal order values will have their relative order determined by ServiceLoader encounter order, which is indeed nondeterministic. The new crypto providers (AuthzClientCryptoProvider with order 100, and existing providers with order 200) have different orders, but if two providers had the same order, the selection would be nondeterministic. This is a valid concern about the design change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Multiple providers with the same priority are now silently selected by ServiceLoader iteration order instead of failing fast, so a classpath containing default and FIPS providers can initialize the wrong crypto backend.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the code changed from throwing an exception when multiple providers exist to silently selecting the one with highest order(). The finding correctly identifies that if multiple providers have the same order value (e.g., both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider return 200), the selection becomes non-deterministic based on ServiceLoader iteration order. This is a valid architectural concern - the code now relies on order() values being unique across providers, but there's no enforcement of this. However, this is not strictly a bug since the providers shown in the diff (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider all return 200, AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100) are not typically on the classpath together, and the design intent appears to be that only one 'real' provider plus the fallback AuthzClient provider would be present.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:60 — A child TLV larger than the enclosing sequence length makes length negative and is accepted, so malformed DER signatures are parsed rather than rejected.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the readSequence() method in ASN1Decoder.java, the length variable is decremented by bytes.length (the actual bytes read), not by the declared length of child TLVs. The code reads: 'length = length - bytes.length'. The bytes.length is the actual size of data read by readNext(), which includes the full TLV encoding. There's no scenario where a child TLV 'larger than the enclosing sequence length' would make length negative and be silently accepted - if readNext() tries to read more bytes than available, the read() method would throw an IOException. The finding misunderstands the code logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:75 — Implementing the broad CryptoProvider contract while most methods throw hides the provider's limited capability from future callers.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements CryptoProvider but throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods (getPemUtils, getCertificateUtils, getKeyPairGen, getKeyFactory, etc.). This is a valid architectural concern - the class implements a broad interface but only supports a subset of operations (getBouncyCastleProvider, getEcdsaCryptoProvider, getKeyStore). While this is intentional for a 'simple crypto provider to be used with the authz-client' as stated in the comment, it could cause runtime failures if callers expect full CryptoProvider functionality. This is a legitimate design/scope concern, not a bug since it's documented behavior, but also not a hallucination as the diff clearly shows this pattern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:56 — Selecting an arbitrary equal-priority provider silently permits a non-FIPS crypto provider when multiple implementations are present.

adjudication.rationale: The finding misreads the diff. The code explicitly sorts providers by order in descending order (reversed()) at line 57, then selects the first one (highest order). The diff shows that FIPS, default, and elytron providers all have order() returning 200, while AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100. This means the 'real' crypto providers (FIPS, default, elytron) will always be selected over the authz-client fallback provider when present. The selection is not 'arbitrary' - it's deterministic based on the order() value. Equal-priority providers would be selected based on ServiceLoader ordering, but this is the expected behavior for providers at the same priority level.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — ES384 and ES512 use the default EC key instead of their required curves, so the round-trip assertion can pass without exercising real 384/521-bit signatures.

adjudication.rationale: The test file shows that a single KeyPair is generated in the constructor using KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() without specifying a curve. This same keyPair is used for all three test methods (testES256, testES384, testES512). The finding correctly identifies that ES384 and ES512 require different curves (P-384 and P-521 respectively) than the default curve used. While the test may still pass because it's testing the ASN1 encoding/decoding round-trip rather than actual signature verification with proper key sizes, this is a legitimate test quality concern - the tests don't properly exercise the signature lengths they claim to test.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — No test exercises AuthzClient.create with the ServiceLoader provider selection, leaving the new crypto initialization path unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds CryptoIntegration.init() call in AuthzClient.create() at line 95, which initializes the crypto provider via ServiceLoader. While there is a new test file ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java that tests the ECDSA algorithm functionality of AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly, there is no test that exercises the AuthzClient.create() method itself to verify the ServiceLoader-based crypto initialization path works correctly. This is a valid observation about missing test coverage for the new initialization logic, though the crypto provider functionality itself is tested.
